name: Maxwell-Boltzmann Most Probable Speed
description: Gives the most probable molecular speed in a gas at thermal equilibrium, the peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution, as the square root of 2kT divided by molecular mass m. It is the speed at which the largest fraction of molecules travel.
notes: Use the mass of one molecule in kg, not molar mass, and temperature in kelvin. This most probable speed is the smallest of the three characteristic speeds, below the mean and rms speeds.

name: Maxwell-Boltzmann Mean Speed
description: Computes the arithmetic mean speed of gas molecules at temperature T from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, as the square root of 8kT divided by pi times molecular mass m. It represents the average of the speed magnitudes of all molecules.
notes: Use molecular mass in kg and temperature in kelvin. The mean speed lies between the most probable and rms speeds, being about 1.128 times the most probable speed.

name: Maxwell-Boltzmann RMS Speed
description: Gives the root-mean-square speed of gas molecules as the square root of 3kT divided by molecular mass m. This speed corresponds directly to the mean translational kinetic energy, since half m times the rms speed squared equals three-halves kT.
notes: Use the mass of one molecule in kg and temperature in kelvin. The rms speed is the largest of the three characteristic speeds and is the physically relevant one for kinetic energy.

name: Mean Translational Kinetic Energy
description: Computes the average translational kinetic energy of a single gas molecule as three-halves times the Boltzmann constant times absolute temperature. It reflects that each of the three translational degrees of freedom carries half kT of energy.
notes: Depends only on temperature, not on molecular mass or gas identity. Temperature must be absolute (kelvin); this is energy per molecule, so multiply by Avogadro's number for a per-mole value.

name: Boltzmann Factor
description: Evaluates the Boltzmann factor, the exponential exp of minus the state energy En divided by kT. It gives the relative probability weight of a microstate at energy En in thermal equilibrium, before normalization by the partition function.
notes: En and kT must share energy units (joules here); only energy differences are physically meaningful. States far above kT in energy are strongly suppressed, while states well below are nearly equally likely.

name: Two-Level Partition Function
description: Computes the partition function of a two-level system, one plus the Boltzmann factor of the upper level with energy gap En. It sums the statistical weights of the ground and excited states and normalizes their occupation probabilities.
notes: The ground state is taken at zero energy, so its weight is 1; En is the gap in joules. At high temperature the value approaches 2 (both levels equally populated) and at low temperature approaches 1.

name: Two-Level System Average Energy
description: Gives the average energy of a two-level system with energy gap En at temperature T, En divided by the quantity exp(En/kT) plus one. It rises from zero at low temperature toward half the gap as both levels become equally populated at high temperature.
notes: Ground state is at zero energy and En is the gap in joules. The form resembles a Fermi-Dirac occupation because a two-state system can hold at most one excitation.

name: Schottky Two-Level Heat Capacity
description: Computes the heat capacity of a two-level system, the Schottky anomaly, from the energy gap En and temperature T. It exhibits a characteristic peak near kT comparable to En, where the system most readily absorbs energy by promoting particles across the gap.
notes: Result is per particle; multiply by the number of particles for a bulk value. The peak occurs around T where kT is roughly En/2.4; the capacity falls to zero at both very low and very high temperatures.

name: Equipartition Theorem Energy
description: Gives the average thermal energy predicted by the equipartition theorem, one-half kT for each of f quadratic degrees of freedom, so half f times kT total. It applies to classical systems where each such degree contributes equally to the energy.
notes: Valid only in the classical high-temperature limit where energy levels are closely spaced; quantum freezing-out at low temperature removes degrees of freedom. Count both translational and, where active, rotational and vibrational degrees in f.

name: Sackur-Tetrode Entropy (Thermal Wavelength Form)
description: Computes the absolute entropy of a monatomic ideal gas via the Sackur-Tetrode equation in thermal-wavelength form, from particle number N, volume V, and thermal de Broglie wavelength lam. It captures how entropy grows with the number of accessible quantum states per particle.
notes: Requires the dilute regime where V/(N·lam^3) is much greater than one, otherwise quantum degeneracy invalidates the formula. The 2.5 additive term comes from the ideal-gas energy and Stirling approximation.

name: Planck Single-Mode Average Energy
description: Gives the average thermal energy of a single electromagnetic mode of frequency f, the Planck occupation times the photon energy hf. It is the Bose-Einstein result that replaces classical equipartition and cures the ultraviolet catastrophe.
notes: This excludes the zero-point energy hf/2. At low frequency (hf much less than kT) it tends to kT, recovering the classical limit; at high frequency it is exponentially suppressed.

name: Maxwell-Boltzmann Occupation Number
description: Computes the classical Maxwell-Boltzmann occupation of a state with energy En and chemical potential mu, exp of minus (En minus mu) divided by kT. It gives the average number of particles in that state in the dilute, non-degenerate limit.
notes: Valid when occupation is much less than one, so quantum statistics reduce to the classical form. En and mu share energy units; states below mu are more populated, above mu less.

name: Dulong-Petit Law
description: States the Dulong-Petit law that the molar heat capacity of a simple crystalline solid is three times the gas constant R. It follows from equipartition, with each atom contributing three kinetic and three potential quadratic degrees of freedom.
notes: Holds only at high temperature, well above the Debye temperature; below it the capacity falls toward zero. The result about 24.9 J/(mol·K) is independent of the specific element.

name: Einstein Model Heat Capacity
description: Computes the molar heat capacity of a solid in the Einstein model, treating N atoms as independent quantum oscillators at a single frequency set by the Einstein temperature theta. It reproduces the Dulong-Petit value at high T and falls off toward low temperature.
notes: Assumes all oscillators share one frequency, so it underestimates the low-temperature capacity compared to the Debye T-cubed behavior. theta and T are in kelvin; the ratio theta/T is dimensionless.

name: Boltzmann Entropy Formula
description: Evaluates Boltzmann's entropy formula, the Boltzmann constant times the natural log of the number of accessible microstates W. It connects the microscopic count of equally probable configurations to the macroscopic thermodynamic entropy.
notes: W must be a pure count (dimensionless) and at least one; ln(W) grows slowly, so entropy scales with the logarithm of the enormous microstate count. Assumes all microstates are equally probable.

name: Ideal Gas Chemical Potential
description: Computes the chemical potential of a monatomic ideal gas as kT times the natural log of the number density n times the cube of the thermal de Broglie wavelength lam. It measures the energy change on adding one particle at fixed temperature and volume.
notes: In the classical dilute regime n·lam^3 is much less than one, so the logarithm is negative, giving a negative chemical potential. n is number density in 1/m^3, not moles.

name: Radiation Energy Density (Stefan-Boltzmann)
description: Gives the energy density of blackbody radiation as four times the Stefan-Boltzmann constant divided by the speed of light, times temperature to the fourth power. It is the total electromagnetic energy per unit volume inside a cavity at temperature T.
notes: Scales steeply with the fourth power of temperature, so doubling T raises the density sixteenfold. Temperature must be absolute (kelvin); this is the integrated density over all wavelengths.

name: Rayleigh-Jeans Law
description: Evaluates the Rayleigh-Jeans spectral radiance, two times the speed of light times kT divided by the fourth power of wavelength lam. It is the classical approximation to blackbody radiation, accurate only at long wavelengths.
notes: Diverges as wavelength shrinks (the ultraviolet catastrophe), so it fails at short wavelengths where Planck's law is required. Valid only when hc/lam is much less than kT.

name: Planck's Law (Spectral Radiance, Wavelength)
description: Computes the spectral radiance of a blackbody per unit wavelength at wavelength lam and temperature T, via Planck's law. It gives the power emitted per unit area, per unit solid angle, per unit wavelength, peaking at a wavelength set by Wien's law.
notes: Wavelength lam is in meters and T in kelvin; the result is per unit wavelength, differing from the per-frequency form. It reduces to Rayleigh-Jeans at long wavelengths and Wien's form at short wavelengths.

name: Planck's Law (Spectral Radiance, Frequency)
description: Computes the spectral radiance of a blackbody per unit frequency at frequency nu and temperature T, via Planck's law. It gives the emitted power per unit area, per unit solid angle, per unit frequency across the thermal spectrum.
notes: This per-frequency form is not simply the wavelength form divided by lam; the two peak at different points. Frequency nu is in Hz and T in kelvin; only positive temperatures are physical.

name: Mean Free Path (Ideal Gas)
description: Estimates the average distance a gas molecule travels between collisions, kT divided by the square root of two times pi times the square of the molecular diameter times pressure. It shows how the mean free path shrinks with higher pressure and larger molecules.
notes: Treats molecules as hard spheres of diameter d and uses the square-root-of-two factor for relative motion. Pressure P is in pascals and T in kelvin; the path grows with temperature at fixed pressure.

name: Molecular Collision Frequency
description: Computes how many collisions a single gas molecule undergoes per second, the square root of two times pi times the square of the molecular diameter times the mean speed times the number density. It links molecular size, speed, and crowding to collision rate.
notes: Uses the hard-sphere collision cross-section with the square-root-of-two factor for relative velocities. n is number density in 1/m^3 (not moles) and vmean the mean molecular speed in m/s.

name: Debye T-Cubed Heat Capacity
description: Gives the low-temperature molar heat capacity of a solid in the Debye model, proportional to the cube of the ratio of temperature to the Debye temperature theta. It captures how lattice vibrations freeze out, driving the capacity to zero as T cubed.
notes: Valid only well below the Debye temperature, typically T less than about theta/10; near or above theta it overestimates and the full Debye integral is needed. T and theta are in kelvin.

name: Langevin Function (Paramagnetism)
description: Evaluates the Langevin function coth(x) minus 1/x, written here with exponentials, describing the classical mean magnetic alignment of dipoles. The argument x is the ratio of magnetic to thermal energy, mu·B divided by kT, and the output ranges from 0 to 1.
notes: For small x it rises linearly as x/3 (Curie law); for large x it saturates toward 1 as dipoles fully align. The coth form has a removable singularity at x=0, so avoid exactly zero input.

name: Entropy of Mixing (Binary)
description: Computes the entropy of mixing for a binary system of N particles with mole fraction x of component A, minus N k times (x ln x plus (1 minus x) ln(1 minus x)). It quantifies the entropy gained when two ideal components are mixed at random.
notes: Mole fraction x must lie strictly between 0 and 1; the entropy is always positive and peaks at x equal to 0.5. Assumes ideal mixing with no interaction energy between components.

name: Quantum Harmonic Oscillator Partition Function
description: Computes the canonical partition function of a quantum harmonic oscillator of frequency f at temperature T, including the zero-point energy in the numerator. It sums the Boltzmann weights over the evenly spaced energy ladder of the oscillator.
notes: The numerator exp(-hf/2kT) reflects the zero-point energy; dropping it shifts the energy origin. At high temperature the value grows as kT/hf, recovering the classical limit.

name: Quantum Harmonic Oscillator Mean Energy
description: Gives the mean thermal energy of a quantum harmonic oscillator of frequency f, the zero-point energy hf/2 plus the Planck occupation times hf. It shows how the oscillator's energy exceeds the classical kT value at low temperature due to zero-point motion.
notes: Includes the zero-point term, so the energy never drops below hf/2 even at absolute zero. At high temperature (kT much greater than hf) it approaches the classical kT.

name: Radiation Pressure (Photon Gas)
description: Computes the pressure exerted by isotropic blackbody radiation, four times the Stefan-Boltzmann constant divided by three times the speed of light, times temperature to the fourth power. It equals one third of the radiation energy density for a photon gas.
notes: Scales with the fourth power of absolute temperature, becoming significant only at very high temperatures such as stellar interiors. Assumes an isotropic photon gas in thermal equilibrium.

name: Ideal Gas Internal Energy (Equipartition)
description: Computes the internal energy of n moles of an ideal gas from equipartition as half f times n times the gas constant R times temperature, where f is the number of active quadratic degrees of freedom per molecule. It gives the total translational and, where relevant, rotational and vibrational energy.
notes: Use f=3 for monatomic, 5 for diatomic at moderate temperature, and more when vibration activates. Valid in the classical regime; quantum modes may be frozen out at low temperature.

name: Density of States (3D Free Electron Gas)
description: Computes the density of states of a three-dimensional free electron gas at energy En in volume V, scaling with the square root of energy. It gives the number of available electronic states per unit energy, a key input for Fermi-gas and solid-state calculations.
notes: This form excludes the factor of two for spin degeneracy; multiply by 2 if spin is counted. Uses the reduced Planck constant hbar and electron mass m in SI units, with energy En in joules.

name: Helmholtz Free Energy from Partition Function
description: Computes the Helmholtz free energy of a system from its canonical partition function Z at temperature T, as F=-k×T×ln(Z), using Boltzmann's constant. It links the microscopic partition function to a macroscopic thermodynamic potential.
notes: Z is the dimensionless canonical partition function and must be positive; temperature T is in kelvin. A larger Z (more accessible microstates) gives a more negative, lower free energy.
